citation.title: Beyond LATE: Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect with an Instrumental Variable

standing_assumptions:
The article is P. M. Aronow and A. Carnegie, ‘Beyond LATE: Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect with an Instrumental Variable’, Political Analysis 21 (2013), pp. 492–506. Printed page = PDF page + 491 (printed p. 492 is PDF p. 1). The official supplement (‘Supporting Information Online Appendix A: Simulation Studies’) is paginated A1–A12 and supplement PDF page k is page Ak. The article states no numbered theorem, proposition or lemma; its formal content is the displayed equations (1)–(14), Assumptions 1–3 and the statements in running text and footnotes quoted below. Everything quoted from the article and the supplement was read from the page images (the staged 110 dpi images and 250 dpi renderings of the same PDF pages). Code and package text have no page image and are transcribed from the staged source files; each such passage is marked.
(S1) Setting and potential outcomes. p. 494 (PDF p. 3), Section 2.2: “We now move to the Neyman-Rubin potential outcomes framework, focusing on the case of a binary IV (or treatment assignment) $Z$ and a binary endogenous treatment variable (or treatment received) $D$. Suppose that we have a sample consisting of $n$ units (indexed $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$) independently drawn with equal probability from some large population of interest. For unit $i$, let $Y_{0i}$ be the outcome if untreated, $D_i = 0$, and let $Y_{1i}$ be the outcome if treated, $D_i = 1$. The treatment effect for a given unit $i$ is the difference between unit $i$’s outcomes in both possible states of the world, $Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}$. Similarly, we may define $D_{0i}$ as the treatment condition of unit $i$ when assigned to control, $Z_i = 0$, and $D_{1i}$ as the treatment condition of unit $i$ when assigned to treatment, $Z_i = 1$. We will show that the causal estimand recovered by IV estimation will not generally be the ATE, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)$, but will instead be the LATE, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0)$.”
(S2) Types. pp. 494–495 (PDF pp. 3–4): “Following Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996), the population may be divided into four groups: always-takers, never-takers, compliers, and defiers. Always-takers are units that receive treatment regardless of whether they are assigned to treatment or control, so that $D_{0i} = 1$ and $D_{1i} = 1$. Conversely, never-takers do not receive treatment regardless of their treatment assignment, so that $D_{0i} = 0$ and $D_{1i} = 0$. Compliers receive treatment if assigned to treatment and do not receive treatment if assigned to control, so that $D_{0i} = 0$ and $D_{1i} = 1$ (or $D_{1i} > D_{0i}$). Defiers receive treatment if assigned to control and do not receive treatment if assigned to treatment, so that $D_{0i} = 1$ and $D_{1i} = 0$ (or $D_{0i} > D_{1i}$).”
(S3) The five IV assumptions. p. 495 (PDF p. 4): “Using an IV estimator, we may estimate the LATE using five assumptions, as explicated by Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996). First, we assume that the exclusion restriction is valid, or that $Z_i$ only affects $Y_i$ through $D_i$. Second, we assume that $Z_i$ to some degree predicts $D_i$. Third, we invoke the stable unit treatment value assumption, which states that the potential outcomes $D_{0i}$, $D_{1i}$, $Y_{0i}$, and $Y_{1i}$ are fixed and unrelated to the particular arrangement of assignment and treatment statuses. Fourth, we assume that the population contains no defiers, i.e., $\Pr(D_0 > D_1) = 0$. Fifth, we assume that $Z_i$ is randomly assigned and thus independent of all potential outcomes.”
(S4) Rendering of (S1)–(S3) used in every target (the article prints no display for it; all validators use it). The observed variables are $D = D_0 + Z(D_1 - D_0)$ and $Y = Y_0 + D(Y_1 - Y_0)$ (exclusion and SUTVA); relevance is $\mathrm{E}(D|Z=1) - \mathrm{E}(D|Z=0) \neq 0$; no defiers is $\Pr(D_0 > D_1) = 0$; random assignment is: $Z$ is independent of $(D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$, and of $(\mathbf{X}, D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$ where covariates appear (p. 496: “so that $\mathbf{X} \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$”), with $0 < \Pr(Z = 1) < 1$. Abbreviations used in the targets and not in the article: $\tau = Y_1 - Y_0$ and $C = \mathbf{1}\{D_1 > D_0\}$.
(S5) SEM framework. p. 493 (PDF p. 2), Section 2.1: “The SEM interpretation of IV estimation posits a linear, additive relationship between an outcome variable ($Y_i$), an endogenous treatment variable ($D_i$), covariates ($Q_{1i}, Q_{2i}....Q_{Ki}$), and an unobserved error term ($u_i$) for each unit $i$, such that $$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \lambda_1 Q_{1i} + \lambda_2 Q_{2i} + .... + \lambda_K Q_{Ki} + u_i. \qquad (1)$$” p. 494 (PDF p. 3): “The first equation, or the “first stage,” is a regression of the endogenous variable on the instrument and covariates: $$D_i = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 Z_i + \delta_1 Q_{1i} + \delta_2 Q_{2i} + .... + \delta_K Q_{Ki} + e_i, \qquad (2)$$ where $e_i$ is a second unobserved error term. [...] Given the model in equations (1) and (2), the SEM IV framework relies on two main assumptions for consistency. First, the correlation between $Z_i$ and $u_i$ must approach zero as $n$ grows. Second, the covariance between $Z_i$ and $D_i$ must converge to a nonzero quantity as $n$ grows. Note, however, that whereas the endogenous variable and covariates in equation (1) are indexed by the subscript $i$, their coefficients (the βs and λs) are not. In other words, the SEM framework assumes constant treatment effects, so that the effect of the treatment is identical for each unit $i$.”
(S6) Compliance score and nested model. p. 496 (PDF p. 5), Section 3.1: “The compliance score is a latent pretreatment covariate that represents the probability of being a complier, conditional on a unit’s pretreatment covariate profile $\mathbf{X}$ (so that $\mathbf{X} \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$). The compliance score for unit $i$, $P_{Ci} = \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i)$, where $\mathbf{x}_i$ is the covariate vector for unit $i$.” Equations (5) and (6), p. 496: $$P_{A,C,i} = \Pr(D_1 > D_0 \cup D_0 = 1|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}), \qquad (5)$$ “where $P_{A,C,i}$ is the conditional probability that unit $i$ is either a complier or an always-taker, $\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}$ is a vector of coefficients to be estimated, and $F(\cdot)$ is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) for an arbitrary distribution. For the purposes of this article, we use a probit model, so $F(\cdot) = \Phi(\cdot)$, where $\Phi$ is the Normal CDF. Second, we similarly specify $$P_{A|A,C,i} = \Pr(D_0 = 1|D_1 > D_0 \cup D_0 = 1, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}), \qquad (6)$$ where $P_{A|A,C,i}$ is the conditional probability that unit $i$ is an always-taker conditional on it being either an always-taker or a complier, and $\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}$ are coefficients to be estimated.” Equation (7), p. 497 (PDF p. 6): “[...] our third assumption: $D_i$ is Bernoulli distributed. Then the likelihood for any unit $i$, $$L(P_{A|A,C,i}, P_{A,C,i}|D, Z) = (P_{A,C,i}(1 - P_{A|A,C,i})Z_i + P_{A,C,i}P_{A|A,C,i})^{D_i}(1 - P_{A,C,i}(1 - P_{A|A,C,i})Z_i - P_{A,C,i}P_{A|A,C,i})^{1-D_i}. \qquad (7)$$ Combining equations (5), (6), and (7), $L(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}|D, Z) = \Pi_{i=1}^{n}((F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))Z_i + F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))^{D_i}(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))Z_i - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))^{1-D_i})$. Thus the ML estimate of $\{\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\}$, $$\{\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \hat\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\} = \underset{\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}},\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}}{\mathrm{argmax}}\left[L(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}|D, Z)\right].$$ After estimating $\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}$ and $\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}$, we may estimate the compliance score for unit $i$, $$\hat{P}_{Ci} = \widehat{\Pr}(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})).$$” (On the page this display is followed by a superscript 3, which is the marker of footnote 3 and not an exponent.) The displays between (6) and (7) that carry the misprints of finding P029-E009 are transcribed in P029-T18.
(S7) ICSW estimator. p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.3: “In the bivariate case (when there are no covariates), the estimator is simple. Define $\hat{w}_{Ci} = 1/\hat{P}_{Ci}$. The ICSW estimator $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} =$ $$\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iY_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i) - (\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)Y_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i))}{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iD_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i) - (\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)D_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i))}.$$ An equivalent estimator may be derived using weighted 2SLS (with weights $\hat{w}_{Ci}$). As with the simple 2SLS case, covariates may also be included to reduce sampling variability without any consequence for the asymptotic bias of the estimator.”
(S8) Assumptions 1–3. p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.4: “In order to consistently estimate the ATE using ICSW, three additional assumptions are required. In the appendix, we demonstrate that ICSW is consistent under Assumptions 1–3, along with the IV assumptions and suitable regularity conditions.” p. 499 (PDF p. 8): “Assumption 1. Latent ignorability of compliance with respect to treatment effect heterogeneity (Frangakis and Rubin 1999; Esterling, Neblo, and Lazer 2011) holds. Assumption 1 entails that, for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$: the expected value of the treatment effect conditional on a covariate profile is equal to the expected value of the treatment effect conditional on a covariate profile and compliance. Put simply, the ATE for all units with a covariate profile $\mathbf{x}$ is equal to the ATE for compliers with a covariate profile $\mathbf{x}$.” p. 500 (PDF p. 9): “Assumption 2. Consistency of $\hat{P}_{Ci}$ for $P_{Ci}$. Assumption 2 amounts to requiring proper specification of the ML estimator. Application of a flexible parametrization of the covariates in $\mathbf{X}$, as is possible with large samples, will necessarily yield consistency, so long as the rate of growth in the number of estimated parameters is sufficiently slow in $n$. In the case of a saturated model and $F(.)$ as the normal CDF, $\hat{P}_{Ci}$ will be unbiased for the conditional probability of compliance.” p. 500: “Assumption 3. For all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$, $\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) \in (\epsilon, 1]$, where $\epsilon > 0$. Note that IV estimation already requires the assumption of nonzero compliance in the full population, and we generalize this assumption to every covariate profile.”
(S9) Appendix notation. p. 504 (PDF p. 13): “For clarity, we remove $i$ subscripts to denote all units subject to any conditional probabilities articulated.” p. 499 (PDF p. 8): “where $f(.)$ is the population pdf of $\mathbf{X}$, $g(.)$ is the subpopulation pdf of $\mathbf{X}$ among compliers, and $\Omega = \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$.” The article writes integrals against the density $f$; the validators’ witnesses use covariates with finitely many values, for which $f(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$ and the integrals are sums.
(S10) Simulation designs (supplement). Supplement p. A1, ‘Baseline Data Generating Process’ (as printed; the misprints are the subject of P029-T19): $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i \sim \mathrm{U}(-1, 1)$; $a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h \sim \mathrm{U}(-2, 2)$; $AC_i = \mathbf{I}[2 + a + bX1_i + cX2_i + dX3_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 3)]$; $A_i = \mathbf{I}[-2 + e + fX1_i + gX2_i + hX3_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 3)]AC_i$; $C_i = AC_i - A_i$; $D_i = D_iZ_i + A_i$; $Y_{0i} = 5AC_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 1)$; $\tau_i = 5 \times (1 + X1_i + X2_i + X3_i)$; $Y_i = Y_{0i} + \tau_iD_i$. “We observe and use $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i$ both as covariates in 2SLS, and for the compliance score model.” Supplement p. A2, under the heading ‘Heterogeneous Treatment Effects, Conditioning on Random Noise’: “Same as baseline, except: $X1'_i, X2'_i, X3'_i \sim U(-1, 1)$ are the observed covariates, which are entirely independent from $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i$.” Under the heading ‘Homogeneous Treatment Effects, Conditioning on Random Noise’: “Same as the previous DGP, except: $\tau_i = 5, \forall i$.”

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.4, the sentence ‘Assumption 1 is less restrictive than the typical ignorability assumption’, set against Assumption 1 and the two displayed ignorability equalities; the witness is the validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 499 (PDF p. 8), paragraph after Assumption 1 beginning ‘Ignorability assumptions, while strong’
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted, p. 499] “However, Assumption 1 may be distinguished from the typical ignorability assumption (Rubin 1978), which requires that both $\mathrm{E}(Y_1|D = 1, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_1|D = 0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$ and $\mathrm{E}(Y_0|D = 1, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_0|D = 0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$. Assumption 1 is less restrictive than the typical ignorability assumption as there is no need to account for baseline selection bias, only the determinants of treatment effect heterogeneity.”
[Reading refuted (the natural reading recorded in validated.json)] Write (I) for the two displayed equalities at a covariate profile $\mathbf{x}$ and (L) for Assumption 1 at $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$. The sentence asserts that, for the same covariates and under the five IV assumptions (S3)–(S4), every law that satisfies (I) satisfies (L).
[Counterexample] One covariate profile ($\mathbf{X} \equiv 1$). A unit's type $T$ is $C$ (complier, $(D_0, D_1) = (0, 1)$), $A$ (always-taker, $(1, 1)$) or $N$ (never-taker, $(0, 0)$) with probabilities $1/2$, $1/4$, $1/4$. $Z$ is independent of $T$ with $\Pr(Z = 1) = 1/2$. $Y_0 = 0$ for every unit; $Y_1 = 1$ if $T = C$ and $Y_1 = 0$ otherwise. $D = D_0 + Z(D_1 - D_0)$ and $Y = Y_0 + D(Y_1 - Y_0)$. The six atoms $(T, Z)$ have probabilities $(C,0)\colon 1/4$, $(C,1)\colon 1/4$, $(A,0)\colon 1/8$, $(A,1)\colon 1/8$, $(N,0)\colon 1/8$, $(N,1)\colon 1/8$.
[Claims] (i) The five IV assumptions hold: $Y$ depends on $Z$ only through $D$; $\mathrm{E}(D|Z = 1) - \mathrm{E}(D|Z = 0) = 3/4 - 1/4 = 1/2$; $\Pr(D_0 > D_1) = 0$; $Z$ is independent of $(D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$.
(ii) $\Pr(D = 1) = \Pr(D = 0) = 1/2$, and $\Pr(T = C|D = 1) = \Pr(T = C|D = 0) = 1/2$.
(iii) (I) holds: $\mathrm{E}(Y_1|D = 1) = \mathrm{E}(Y_1|D = 0) = 1/2$ and $\mathrm{E}(Y_0|D = 1) = \mathrm{E}(Y_0|D = 0) = 0$. Moreover the pair $(Y_0, Y_1)$ is independent of $D$.
(iv) (L) fails: $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0) = 1/2$ and $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0) = 1$.
(v) Assumption 3 holds with $\epsilon = 1/4$, since $\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X}) = 1/2$.
(vi) $\mathrm{E}(Y|Z = 1) = 1/2$ and $\mathrm{E}(Y|Z = 0) = 0$, so the right side of (3) equals $1$; the compliance score is the constant $1/2$, so the inverse-score weights are the constant $2$ and cancel, and the population value of the ICSW ratio is also $1$, while $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0) = 1/2$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.4, comparison of Assumption 1 with the typical ignorability assumption, corrected: the two conditions are not ordered in general; the typical condition implies Assumption 1 under one-sided noncompliance
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text (Sol's smallest repair in validated.json, identical to prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Assumption 1 and the typical ignorability assumption displayed here impose different restrictions and are not generally ordered. Assumption 1 permits baseline selection bias, provided that the conditional average treatment effect for compliers equals that for the full population.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] As in P029-T1, (I) at $\mathbf{x}$ is the pair $\mathrm{E}(Y_d|D = 1, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_d|D = 0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$ for $d = 0, 1$, and (L) at $\mathbf{x}$ is $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$.
(a) [(I) does not imply (L)] There is a law satisfying the five IV assumptions (S3)–(S4), with positive probabilities of compliers, always-takers and never-takers, in which (I) holds and (L) fails: the law of P029-T1.
(b) [(L) does not imply (I)] Take the type law and the assignment of P029-T1 ($\Pr(T = C, A, N) = (1/2, 1/4, 1/4)$, $Z$ independent of $T$, $\Pr(Z = 1) = 1/2$, one covariate profile) with $Y_0 = 1$ if $T = A$ and $Y_0 = 0$ otherwise, and $Y_1 = Y_0 + 1$. Then the five IV assumptions hold; $Y_1 - Y_0 = 1$ for every unit, so (L) holds with both sides equal to $1$; and $\mathrm{E}(Y_0|D = 1) = 1/2 \neq 0 = \mathrm{E}(Y_0|D = 0)$ and $\mathrm{E}(Y_1|D = 1) = 3/2 \neq 1 = \mathrm{E}(Y_1|D = 0)$, so both equalities of (I) fail.
(c) [The implication that does hold: one-sided noncompliance] Let $(\mathbf{X}, D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1, Z)$ be random variables with $D_0, D_1, Z \in \{0, 1\}$, $\mathrm{E}|Y_0| < \infty$, $\mathrm{E}|Y_1| < \infty$, $D = D_0 + Z(D_1 - D_0)$, and $Z$ independent of $(\mathbf{X}, D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$ with $0 < \Pr(Z = 1) < 1$. Suppose $\Pr(D_0 = 0) = 1$ (no unit assigned to control receives treatment). Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a covariate value with $\Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) > 0$ and $\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) > 0$. If (I) holds at $\mathbf{x}$, then (L) holds at $\mathbf{x}$. (Proof idea of the validator: here $\{D = 1\} = \{D_1 > D_0, Z = 1\}$, so $\mathrm{E}(Y_d|D = 1, \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_d|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{x})$; by (I) and the law of total expectation $\mathrm{E}(Y_d|\mathbf{x})$ equals the same common value; subtract $d = 0$ from $d = 1$.)

canonical_claim.note: Repair cost recorded by Sol: weaker_conclusion; no assumption, estimand, formula or number changes. Part (b) is the article's own correct point (Assumption 1 tolerates baseline selection); part (a) is what the printed ordering misses; part (c) records the scope in which the printed ordering is true, and is not the repair, since the method and the Albertson–Lawrence application cover two-sided noncompliance. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.4, the sentence ‘More generally, even if treatment effects are heterogeneous, but still statistically independent of compliance, Assumption 1 would necessarily be satisfied, and both 2SLS and ICSW would be consistent for the ATE’; the two witnesses are the validator's and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 499 (PDF p. 8), last sentence of the paragraph beginning ‘We can describe sufficient conditions for and consequences of Assumption 1’
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted, p. 499] “More generally, even if treatment effects are heterogeneous, but still statistically independent of compliance, Assumption 1 would necessarily be satisfied, and both 2SLS and ICSW would be consistent for the ATE.”
[Readings refuted] (M) ‘independent’ read as marginal independence of $\tau = Y_1 - Y_0$ from the compliance type: witness (A) shows that Assumption 1 can then fail and that the population limit of ICSW, computed with the true compliance scores, differs from the ATE. (X) ‘independent’ read as independence conditional on $\mathbf{X}$: witness (B) shows that the limit of 2SLS (the LATE) can then differ from the ATE.
[Common construction] A binary covariate $X \in \{0, 1\}$; $(C, \tau, X)$ has one of the joint laws below, with $C, \tau \in \{0, 1\}$; $H \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ independent of $(C, \tau, X)$; $A = (1 - C)H$; $D_0 = A$, $D_1 = A + C$ (so $C = 1$: complier; $C = 0, H = 1$: always-taker; $C = 0, H = 0$: never-taker; no defiers); $Y_0 = 0$, $Y_1 = \tau$; $Z \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ independent of $(C, \tau, X, H)$; $D = A + CZ$, $Y = \tau D$. Notation: $f(x) = \Pr(X = x)$, $P_C(x) = \Pr(C = 1|X = x)$, $\mu(x) = \mathrm{E}(\tau|C = 1, X = x)$. For a weight $w(X) > 0$ the weighted Wald ratio is $\theta_w = \dfrac{\mathrm{E}(wY|Z=1)/\mathrm{E}(w|Z=1) - \mathrm{E}(wY|Z=0)/\mathrm{E}(w|Z=0)}{\mathrm{E}(wD|Z=1)/\mathrm{E}(w|Z=1) - \mathrm{E}(wD|Z=0)/\mathrm{E}(w|Z=0)}$; $w \equiv 1$ gives the right side of (3) and $w = 1/P_C(X)$ gives the population ICSW ratio.
(A) [Marginal independence; Assumption 1 and the ICSW conclusion fail] $\Pr(C = c, \tau = t, X = x)$: $(0,0,0)\colon 3/16$; $(0,0,1)\colon 1/16$; $(0,1,0)\colon 3/16$; $(0,1,1)\colon 1/16$; $(1,0,0)\colon 3/16$; $(1,0,1)\colon 1/16$; $(1,1,0)\colon 1/16$; $(1,1,1)\colon 3/16$. Claims: (A1) $C$ and $\tau$ are independent $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ variables, and $\tau$ is independent of the full type (complier, always-taker, never-taker); $\tau$ is not constant. (A2) $f(0) = 5/8$, $f(1) = 3/8$; $P_C(0) = 2/5$, $P_C(1) = 2/3$, so Assumption 3 holds with $\epsilon = 1/3$; $\Pr(D_1 = 1|X = 0) = 7/10$, $\Pr(D_0 = 1|D_1 = 1, X = 0) = 3/7$, $\Pr(D_1 = 1|X = 1) = 5/6$, $\Pr(D_0 = 1|D_1 = 1, X = 1) = 1/5$, all in $(0, 1)$. (A3) $\mathrm{E}(\tau|X = 0) = 2/5$ but $\mu(0) = 1/4$; $\mathrm{E}(\tau|X = 1) = 2/3$ but $\mu(1) = 3/4$: Assumption 1 fails at both profiles. (A4) $\mathrm{E}(\tau) = 1/2$ and $\mathrm{E}(\tau|C = 1) = 1/2$; $\theta_1 = (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2$. (A5) With $w = 1/P_C(X)$ (weights $5/2$ and $3/2$): $\mathrm{E}(w) = 17/8$; the weighted outcome difference is $7/34$ and the weighted treatment difference is $8/17$; $\theta_{1/P_C} = 7/16 = f(0)\mu(0) + f(1)\mu(1) \neq 1/2$.

(iii) [ICSW with the true scores] $\theta_{1/P_C} = \sum_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{x})\mu(\mathbf{x})$.

Retain heterogeneous scoring against row 1. Exact historical numerical corrections require the simulation arrays or a rerun.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis]
(a) [The target] In the design ‘Homogeneous Treatment Effects, Conditioning on Random Noise’ the potential outcomes of unit $i$ are $Y_{0i}$ and $Y_{1i} = Y_{0i} + 5$, so $Y_{1i} - Y_{0i} = 5$ for every unit; hence for every sample of size $n \ge 1$ the sample average effect $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (Y_{1i} - Y_{0i})$ equals $5$, the population ATE $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)$ equals $5$, and $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0) = 5$ whenever $\Pr(D_1 > D_0) > 0$.
(b) [The corrected statistic] For estimator $j$ and replicates $r = 1, \ldots, R$: $\mathrm{RMSE}_j = \sqrt{\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(t_{jr} - 5)^2}$.
(c) [The coded benchmark] Let $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, be $3n$ independent $\mathrm{U}(-1, 1)$ variables and $B = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}5(1 + X1_i + X2_i + X3_i)$. Then $\mathrm{E}(U) = 0$ and $\mathrm{E}(U^2) = 1/3$ for $U \sim \mathrm{U}(-1, 1)$, $\mathrm{E}(B) = 5$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B) = 25/n$.
(d) [Exact relation between the two squared errors] For all real $t$ and $B$: $(t - B)^2 - (t - 5)^2 = (B - 5)^2 - 2(t - 5)(B - 5)$. Hence for any finite run $\frac{1}{R}\sum_r (t_{jr} - B_r)^2 - \frac{1}{R}\sum_r (t_{jr} - 5)^2 = \frac{1}{R}\sum_r (B_r - 5)^2 - \frac{2}{R}\sum_r (t_{jr} - 5)(B_r - 5)$, and if $t$ and $B$ have finite second moments with $\mathrm{E}(B) = 5$, $\mathrm{E}(t - B)^2 - \mathrm{E}(t - 5)^2 = \mathrm{Var}(B) - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(t, B)$.
(e) [The sign of the discrepancy is not determined by $\mathrm{Var}(B)$] There are admissible inputs with $(t - B)^2 - (t - 5)^2 = 1$ and admissible inputs with $(t - B)^2 - (t - 5)^2 = -1$: P029-T5(b) and (c).

Optionally, bootstrap the entire estimation process for the purpose of hypothesis testing and constructing confidence intervals.”; argument `weights`: “Observation weights.” Read with the source below, this says that the compliance model is fitted with the supplied observation weights and, in each bootstrap replicate, refitted to that replicate's weights.
[Package source, transcribed from the staged files] One-sided branch (compliance.score.R, lines 43–48): `fit <- glm(D ~ W, df, subset = (Z == 1), family = binomial(link="probit"))`; `C.score <- predict(fit, newdata = df, type = "response")`. Two-sided objective (lines 88–91): `p.D <- p.AC * (1 - p.A) * Z + p.AC * p.A`; `p.D <- pmax(pmin(p.D, 1 - 1e-5), 1e-5)`; `return(-sum(log((p.D)^D * (1 - p.D)^(1 - D) * weights)))`. Bootstrap (icsw.tsls.R, lines 29–32): `weights.r <- rexp(n.obs, 1) # Bayesian bootstrap`; `coefs.r <- icsw.tsls.fit(D, X, Y, Z, W, weights = weights * weights.r, ...`.
[Reading in real arithmetic] With $L_i(\theta) = p_i(\theta)^{D_i}(1 - p_i(\theta))^{1-D_i}$ and $p_i(\theta) \in [10^{-5}, 1 - 10^{-5}]$ the modeled receipt probability of (7), the two-sided objective that is minimized is $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; w) = -\sum_i \log(L_i(\theta)\,w_i)$. The one-sided fit maximizes the unweighted probit likelihood of $D$ on the units with $Z_i = 1$, whatever $w$ is.
[Claims]
(i) For positive finite weights, $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; w) = Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; \mathbf{1}) - \sum_i \log w_i$ for every $\theta$; hence the set of minimizers of $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\cdot; w)$ is the same for every positive $w$, and equals that of the unweighted negative log likelihood.
(ii) If $w_i = 0$ for some $i$ and the other weights are positive, then $L_i(\theta)w_i = 0$ and, with $\log 0 = -\infty$, $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; w) = +\infty$ for every $\theta$.
(iii) [One-sided witness; the final estimate changes] Sixteen observations $(W, Z, D, \text{weight})$: for $W = 0$: four with $(Z, D) = (0, 0)$ and weight $1$; one with $(1, 1)$ and weight $9$; three with $(1, 0)$ and weight $1$; for $W = 1$: four with $(0, 0)$ and weight $1$; three with $(1, 1)$ and weight $9$; one with $(1, 0)$ and weight $1$. $Y = D(1 + W)$. The compliance model has an intercept and the binary predictor $W$ (saturated). The unweighted fit on the $Z = 1$ units gives scores $(C(0), C(1)) = (1/4, 3/4)$, whether or not the weights are supplied. The weighted maximum likelihood fit gives $(9/12, 27/28) = (3/4, 27/28)$. [Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Let $L_i(\theta) \in (0, 1]$ be the Bernoulli likelihood contribution of observation $i$ ($L_i = p_i^{D_i}(1 - p_i)^{1-D_i}$ with $p_i(\theta) \in (0, 1)$), and $w_i \ge 0$ finite weights. [Printed statement] p. 501: “We see that compliers are more likely to have voted previously, be members of a major party, and identify as white (see the supplementary appendix for a correlation matrix between the estimated compliance score and covariates).” Supplement Table A7 (“Compliance Score / Covariate Correlation Matrix for Green, Gerber and Nickerson (2003). Size; White; Black; Voted 00; Voted 99; Voted Pri.; Age; Age M.; Dem; Rep; Ind: $1.00$; $0.37$; $0.61$; $0.32$; $0.40$; $0.43$; $0.25$; $0.23$; $-0.55$; $0.38$; $0.31$; $-0.47$.
[Inference refuted] That the recorded data determine the sign of the pooled association between being a complier and identifying as white. In the staged data the indicator ‘White’ is $1$ exactly for records whose race field is ‘W’; the race field is blank for every record outside Raleigh.
[Counts from the staged data (the validator's; recomputed from the staged file when this list was fixed)] $N = 18933$ records, of which $4660$ are in Raleigh ($3884$ with race W, $776$ with another or an unknown code) and $14273$ are in the five other cities, all with a blank race field. $8721$ records are assigned to treatment and $2551$ of them were contacted; no control record was contacted. Among the Raleigh records assigned to treatment, $602$ of the $1370$ recorded W and $160$ of the $315$ others were contacted.
[Sign identity] For a finite population of $N$ units with binary variables $W$ and $C$, let $n_W = \#\{W = 1\}$, $n_C = \#\{C = 1\}$ and $n_{11} = \#\{W = 1, C = 1\}$, with $0 < n_W < N$. Then, with population (denominator $N$) moments, $\mathrm{Cov}(C, W) = \dfrac{Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W}{N^2}$ and $\mathrm{E}(C|W = 1) - \mathrm{E}(C|W = 0) = \dfrac{Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W}{n_W(N - n_W)}$; both have the sign of $Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W$.
[Two complete populations compatible with the same recorded data] In both, each record assigned to treatment has $C_i$ equal to its recorded contact indicator and each control record has $C_i = 0$, with $D_i(0) = 0$ and $D_i(1) = C_i$ (so the recorded $D_i = Z_iC_i$ is reproduced, there are no defiers and noncompliance is one-sided), and $Y_i(0) = Y_i(1)$ equal to the recorded outcome; every recorded race code is kept, and the $21$ Raleigh records with an unknown code are non-white. World A: every record with a blank race field is non-white. World B: every record with a blank race field is white.
(A) $N = 18933$, $n_W = 3884$, $n_C = 2551$, $n_{11} = 602$: $Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W = 1489582 > 0$ and $\mathrm{E}(C|W = 1) - \mathrm{E}(C|W = 0) = \dfrac{744791}{29225158} > 0$.
(B) $N = 18933$, $n_W = 3884 + 14273 = 18157$, $n_C = 2551$, $n_{11} = 602 + (2551 - 762) = 2391$: $Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W = -1049704 < 0$ and $\mathrm{E}(C|W = 1) - \mathrm{E}(C|W = 0) = -\dfrac{131213}{1761229} < 0$.
Hence the recorded data are compatible both with compliers being more likely, and with compliers being less likely, to be white than non-compliers.

So ‘compliers are more likely to be white’ and ‘white units are more likely to be compliers’ are both equivalent to $Nn_{11} > n_Cn_W$.
(b) [What the recorded labels show where they exist] Among the $1685$ Raleigh records assigned to treatment, where contact reveals compliance, the contact rate of records with race W is $602/1370$ and that of the other records is $160/315$; $\dfrac{602}{1370} - \dfrac{160}{315} = -\dfrac{2957}{43155} < 0$. canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted, p. 500] “In the case of a saturated model and $F(.)$ as the normal CDF, $\hat{P}_{Ci}$ will be unbiased for the conditional probability of compliance.”
[Reading] $\hat{P}_{Ci}$ is the maximum likelihood estimate of Section 3.1 (S6). In a saturated model each covariate stratum has its own pair $(P_{A,C}, P_{A|A,C})$; write $p = P_{A,C}$ for the modeled $\Pr(D = 1|Z = 1)$ and $q = P_{A,C}P_{A|A,C}$ for the modeled $\Pr(D = 1|Z = 0)$ in the stratum, so that the compliance score is $p - q$ and the model imposes $q \le p$. With finite probit coefficients $0 < q < p < 1$; boundary fits are taken in the closure $\{0 \le q \le p \le 1\}$, with $0^0 = 1$ (the convention under which the validator evaluates the claim).
[Counterexample] One covariate stratum. Types: always-taker, complier, never-taker with probabilities $1/4$, $1/2$, $1/4$ (so the true $P_{A,C} = 3/4$ and $P_{A|A,C} = 1/3$ are interior and the true compliance score is $1/2$). One unit is observed in each assignment arm, independently; their receipts are $d_1 \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(3/4)$ in the arm $Z = 1$ and $d_0 \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/4)$ in the arm $Z = 0$. The likelihood (7) of the two observations is $L(p, q) = p^{d_1}(1 - p)^{1 - d_1}q^{d_0}(1 - q)^{1 - d_0}$.
[Claims] (i) On $\{0 \le q \le p \le 1\}$ the maximum of $L$ and its maximizer are: $(d_1, d_0) = (0, 0)$: $L = 1$ at $(p, q) = (0, 0)$; $(0, 1)$: $L = 1/4$ at $(1/2, 1/2)$; $(1, 0)$: $L = 1$ at $(1, 0)$; $(1, 1)$: $L = 1$ at $(1, 1)$. The inequalities are certified by the identities $1 - (1 - p)(1 - q) = p + (1 - p)q$, $\tfrac14 - (1 - p)q = (p - \tfrac12)^2 + (1 - p)(p - q)$, $1 - p(1 - q) = (1 - p) + pq$ and $1 - pq = (1 - p) + p(1 - q)$, whose right sides are nonnegative on the region.
(ii) Hence the estimated compliance score $\hat{c} = \hat{p} - \hat{q}$ equals $1$ when $(d_1, d_0) = (1, 0)$ and $0$ otherwise.
(iii) The four outcomes have probabilities $3/16$, $1/16$, $9/16$, $3/16$ (in the order of (i)), so $\mathrm{E}(\hat{c}) = 9/16 \neq 1/2$; the bias is $1/16$. The unconstrained difference $d_1 - d_0$ has expectation $1/2$.
(iv) [Not a one-observation artifact] With five units in each arm, $k_1 \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(5, 1/2)$ and $k_0 \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(5, 3/10)$ independent (true score $1/5$) and $\hat{c} = \max(k_1/5 - k_0/5, 0)$ (P029-T14(a)): $\mathrm{E}(\hat{c}) = 15659/64000$, a bias of $2859/64000$, and $\Pr(k_1 < k_0) = 257079/1600000$.
